recent_candidates.title: AI agents still act like ‘Day 1 employees,’ Glean CEO says
recent_candidates.author: Ben Kesslen
recent_candidates.excerpt: AI agents are nowhere near having the “context” to outperform skilled humans, Glean CEO Arvind Jain said Monday. “When you deploy AI agents, and you actually point them to the right data and knowledge that they need to do their work, they still come and act more like Day 1 employees,” Jain told the editor-in-chief of The Verge, Nilay Patel, at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “That’s the gap that needs to close before we can come and talk about fancy things like job elimination.” Jain, who co-founded the AI platform Glean in 2019, said “nobody’s anywhere close” to building AI systems capable of replacing experienced workers. Glean, he said, is meant to bring “tacit knowledge” and experience with a company to its internal AI systems, to combat that “Day 1 employee” problem. Despite AI’s limitations, Jain also said companies are under “enormous pressure” to adopt it. That may be one reason, he said, for recent high-level technological disruptions, like the outages this week reported by banks and airlines. “Sometimes businesses didn’t get time to actually set the right foundation” before rolling out AI tools, Jain said. Jain also predicted a future in which around 90% of work can be done by open-source and non-frontier AI models, though the remaining “10% of the tasks will actually still consume the majority of your AI spend.” — Ben Kesslen

As in previous administrations, the current Trump administration has assembled a collection of envoys largely based on region and policy imperative. Regions like the Middle East, South and Central Asia, and the Arctic all have special envoys, as do specific countries like Syria, Belarus, Greenland, and Ukraine (currently vacant). recent_candidates.author: Scott Shapiro
recent_candidates.excerpt: I was sitting in a classroom at Yale University when I saw the Future. The class was called Security, Law and Logic, which I co-taught with Ruzica Piskac , a computer science professor at Yale. Piskac was lecturing that day on theorem provers and model checkers, tools that put mathematical logic to work. She explained how computer scientists use them to verify the safety and security of software. Remember the “Blue Screen of Death”? You’d be working on your computer, minding your own business, when suddenly the screen turned blue, Windows crashed, and everything you hadn’t saved was gone. One culprit was faulty device drivers, the software that allows Windows to communicate with hardware such as printers and graphics cards. Microsoft began using a model checker to catch these bugs before the drivers shipped. Instead of just FAFO , Microsoft had the checker search systematically for ways the driver could violate the rules for interacting with Windows. The idea was to find the crash before the crash found you. But what if you used the same tools to test the safety and security of rules themselves, not just computer code that implements them? Suppose everyone responsible for following the rules followed them exactly. Could an attacker still produce an outcome the rules were designed to prevent? If so, the bug isn’t in the software. recent_candidates.excerpt: In 1959, one of the most significant events of the Khrushchev Thaw took place in Moscow’s Sokolniki Park: the American National Exhibition. In its pavilions, Soviet citizens could explore American art and see how Americans lived: what cars they drove, what kitchens they cooked in, and what beds they slept in. But what the exhibition in Sokolniki is remembered for most is not its works of art and design, but the “Kitchen Debate.” On July 24, U.S. Vice President Richard Nixon arrived for the exhibition’s opening and met with Soviet Communist Party First Secretary Nikita Khrushchev. Together, the two toured a model American house that, according to its creators, any U.S. citizen could afford. When the two politicians stepped into the kitchen, Khrushchev had to make the case for the Soviet system while surrounded by unprecedented marvels: a refrigerator, a washing machine, and a dishwasher. Architecture journalist Asya Zolnikova tells the story of what that American house looked like, what else was at the Sokolniki exhibition, and what impact it had on U.S.-Russian relations. In the Soviet Union, every question got hashed out in the kitchen. And it was in a kitchen that perhaps the most important conversation of the Cold War took place: a canary-yellow General Electric kitchen, shipped to Moscow along with other comforts of American middle-class life for the American National Exhibition in Moscow (ANEM) at Sokolniki. Users could erase their data instantly with a panic PIN , and repeated incorrect password attempts could trigger deletion. The phones could also be wiped remotely . French and Dutch authorities, with support from Europol and Eurojust, had gained access to EncroChat’s network and were intercepting millions of messages, including some in real time. When EncroChat discovered the penetration in June 2020, it warned its users to dispose of their phones. recent_candidates.title: The sorry decline of Central Park
recent_candidates.author: Nicole Gelinas
recent_candidates.excerpt: Last week, a New York court had to adjourn an arraignment hearing for Jonathan Robles — the man accused of killing a 63-year-old artist in Central Park — after a psychiatric evaluation concluded that he was unfit to stand trial. In September, the 36-year-old Robles beat his victim, Frances Lee Rogers, 20 times with a stick, causing massive internal bleeding. Rogers thus became the park’s first murder victim since 2022. The media image of the park, of course, is still that of a verdant oasis — a perception reinforced by events like the New York City Marathon that saw more than 60,000 runners streaming beneath Central Park’s fall foliage across the finish line. The exuberance of the runners and spectators, set against the brochure-perfect leafy backdrop, masked a darker reality: a breakdown in public safety and order within Manhattan’s most precious asset. The growing toll of violent deaths, as well as injuries and unpleasant encounters, are evidence that New York City has splintered into an array of unrepresentative but powerful special interests, which no longer come together to approximate a public interest. The numbers tell one story: according to the New York Police Department, park visitors have fallen victim to 93 felonies this year, as of the first week in November, nearly 18% higher than last year and the highest figure in 16 years. From the mid-1990s until 2019, serious crime in Central Park trended downward. But after a lull in 2020 and 2021, crime has gone back up.

Nobody even knew what had gone wrong. In theory, these two incidents have nothing to do with each other. And, as a matter of fact, representatives from both Microsoft and the US secretary of Homeland Security have explicitly denied the two being connected. Superficially, of course, this is true: the Microsoft outage did not damage the FAA equipment. Yet, on a deeper level, these two crises are in fact linked. recent_candidates.excerpt: Before the Downfall: Hitler’s Years in the Wolf’s Lair, Felix Bohr, translated by Jessica Spengler, Polity Books, £25 Go to the modern history section of any bookshop in Germany and you will find lots of books by Anglophone authors. Richard Evans, Ian Kershaw, Christopher Clark: they are all bigger celebrities in Germany than in their home countries, and bigger over there than their German counterparts. Why is this the case? It is not as if Germany has no historians to boast of. Anyone who writes about German history will feel an immense debt of gratitude to all who have toiled away at their Habilitationsschriften and given themselves over to long-term collaborative projects, all handsomely resourced by a state that values scholarship highly. And yet, the closer one gets to t he years 1933-1945 , and the greater the need for an engaging and readable synthesis, the less the German historian seems able to offer. recent_candidates.excerpt: One of my heroes was lost on a mountain in Maine. Not just any mountain, but The Greatest Mountain— Katahdin , named by the Abenaki. The highest mountain in the state shares with Downeast coastal Quoddy Head the first light each day in our continental U.S. This mountain has a distinctive profile, standing long and lone. Its two, often cloud-swathed, peaks are connected by a narrow hikers path of eroding stones called the Knife Edge, some only places 2-3 ft. wide, some places dropping off almost sheer to the distant valley below. Beneath the primary summit of Baxter is a plateau where my hero spent part of his first day wandering in clouds, once falling through krumholtz . Originally published in 1978, Lost on a Mountain in Maine by Donn Fendler shares his struggles in the vast wilderness on Mt. Katahdin. La estrategia asume que el multilateralismo, aunque indispensable, ya no puede ser el único fundamento de la aproximación europea. La UE aspira a ser una “potencia geopolítica” en el Ártico, pero su naturaleza no estatal restringe esa ambición. La principal novedad política de la nueva estrategia es el marco de Vecindad Septentrional. recent_candidates.title: Data center industry should repurpose older infrastructure, SambaNova CEO says
recent_candidates.author: Jake Angelo
recent_candidates.excerpt: Data center builders must adapt to AI pushback, SambaNova CEO Rodrigo Liang said on Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. One way to do that, Liang said, is to repurpose existing data centers. This approach “disrupts the communities less,” he told Semafor’s Liz Rappaport. AI backlash has presented a formidable obstacle for the data center buildout. People voted to limit data center development in 40 out of 41 ballot measures across the US on Election Day, and some newly elected Democratic leaders have laid out plans to pass data-center moratoria. Existing data centers tend to be much smaller than the massive ones being built for AI, and repurposing old infrastructure will require the industry to be “much more energy-efficient in the chips that we build,” Liang said. Still, he said, it’s good for the industry to get more value out of what it has available now. “To distribute the data center into existing environments where power already exists, the infrastructure already exists, the cooling already exists and fits within the ecosystem — it’s not a bad way to do it,” he said. Compute is a precious resource for companies right now. Voice AI company ElevenLabs CEO Mati Staniszewski told Rappaport that “compute constraint” in the near term is a real possibility. — Jake Angelo

recent_candidates.title: Mary Peltola unseats Sen. Dan Sullivan, giving Dems a wider Senate majority
recent_candidates.author: By Lisa Kashinsky
recent_candidates.excerpt: Former Rep. Mary Peltola ousted GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska — the first time in 18 years a Democrat has won a Senate race in the state. Peltola was one of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer’s top recruits for the cycle. She overpowered a Republican rescue mission for Sullivan and allegations of misconduct against her from former staffers to flip a state President Donald Trump won by 13 points in 2024. Her victory continues the blue wave born from voters’ frustrations at high costs and the Trump administration. Peltola will return to Washington, where she will become the first Alaska Native to serve in the Senate after previously holding the same distinction in the House. Her campaign had projected confidence about her path to victory as the vote count dragged on in a far-flung, rural state with long grace periods for late-arriving ballots. But her win was not without tumult. Trump’s Department of Justice sued to try to stop the certification if Sullivan lost, claiming voters could be confused by his same-name challenger. The president went so far as to call for votes for retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan and another longshot candidate in the four-way, all-party contest to be transferred to the incumbent. The Justice Department also started probing efforts to recruit Dan J. Sullivan after a New York Times report suggesting members of Peltola’s campaign and Senate Democrats’ campaign arm were involved. Both had previously denied involvement.

recent_candidates.title: Access to Generative AI: Privilege or Right?
recent_candidates.author: Ziad Reslan, Kim Malfacini, Kevin Chen
recent_candidates.excerpt: Most technologies viewed as critical necessities today began as luxuries enjoyed by a wealthy and privileged elite. In some cases, technology evolved over time to become widespread and indispensable to modern life. A technology’s progression from privilege to right often involves an evolution in the way in which the technology is perceived, regulated, and accessed. What begins as expensive, novel, and access-limited can later become cheap, ubiquitous, and indispensable. This evolution may be evident not only in how consumers act but also in the services organizations and governments prioritize. Nonprofit organizations focused on serving the basic needs of the unhoused previously provided food and shelter and now, increasingly, provide access to cheap mobile phones. Several decades ago, internet access started as a U.S. Department of Defense research experiment with highly limited access. Now, the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals include pursuing universal, affordable internet access in the least developed countries. What were once niche technologies have become, for all intents and purposes, essential to full participation in modern society. Use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has seen a meteoric rise since the launch of ChatGPT in November 2022. In the early 2020s, access to the technology was largely gated behind application programming interfaces (APIs) and limited to wealthy corporations, select government agencies, and tech-forward early adopters.

Asserting control over both shores of the Øresund, Valdemar had an important chokepoint in his hands. In 1361 he sacked the Hanseatic town of Visby and then routed a Hanseatic fleet off Helsingborg in 1362. The Confederation of Cologne was led by the cities of the Hansa, though it took on crowned allies in Sweden, Mecklenburg and Holstein. In 1368, its fleet sacked Copenhagen, and Valdemar left his kingdom in search of new allies. He never found them. Under the Peace of Stralsund of 1370, the towns won free trade across the Baltic, the fortresses of Malmö, Helsingborg, Skanör and Falsterbo for 15 years with two thirds of their revenues, and a veto over candidates for the Danish throne. Maritime coercion is making a comeback. After centuries of naval domination by Britain and, later, the United States, a variety of actors are seeking to use their control of geographic chokepoints to create new political dependencies and force others into strategic compromises. Those who value freedom of navigation and free trade can re-learn a lesson or two from the Hanseatic model. The Hansa – at its height a loose association of close to 200 towns – had no standing navy, no common treasury and no sovereign. Yet it kept its sea lanes open for almost three centuries.

recent_candidates.excerpt: Having read and profited from Peco Gaskovski’s 2023 novel, Exogenesis , I thought I knew what to expect from its new prequel, The Last Upheaval . I expect prequels to fill in the blanks, to do my backstory imagining for me, and to tell me methodically why the book it precedes paints the picture that it does. I do not expect it to challenge or surprise me. But Upheaval turned out to be something more than an explanatory tour. Challenge and surprise, this book does. To begin with, I did not expect the demon, the “fiend,” the yellow-eyed figure who haunts the protagonist’s psyche and sometimes emerges fully and factually into his physical life. This figure passes in and out of the story, appearing rarely but powerfully, somewhat like Weyland Smith in the Buccmaster Trilogy (which Tessa Carman recently considered in these pages along with Exogenesis ). He lurks within the story with both vicious delight and foreknowledge of the plot. He is real, that is for sure—even if his target, an avoidant tech writer named Sol Mereman, is not always sure what else is. Christian faith, in which the demon may meet his match, is also a major theme of the book, and a complex one. recent_candidates.author: Sinc
recent_candidates.excerpt: En la segunda Edad del Hierro, hace más de 2 000 años, Menorca (en las Islas Baleares) tenía sus ritos y costumbres propias. Una de ellas tenía que ver con la tradición funeraria local en la que enterraban a los difuntos en cuevas excavadas en la roca donde los vivos se despedían de sus seres queridos mediante ofrendas de animales, líquidos o alimentos perecederos dentro de pequeñas vasijas. Hasta ahora, el contenido de esos recipientes de cerámica era algo desconocido. Un estudio de la Universidad Autónoma de Barcelona (UAB) ha desvelado cuáles fueron los productos depositados , además de identificar un ritual autóctono de la isla balear. recent_candidates.title: La adicción al móvil se duplicó entre 2016 y 2023 en España, lo que aumentó la depresión
recent_candidates.author: Sinc
recent_candidates.excerpt: No cabe duda de que las nuevas tecnologías y dispositivos , como los smartphones , han traído muchos avances a nuestras vidas. Desde controlar nuestro estado de salud, mantenernos comunicados con nuestros amigos y familiares o consultar información, hay pocas cosas que ya no podamos hacer a través de ellos. El smartphone facilita la comunicación y el acceso a la información , pero ¿qué sucede cuando su uso deja de estar bajo nuestro control? ¿Puede afectar a nuestra salud emocional y a nuestras relaciones sociales? recent_candidates.excerpt: El fabricante estadounidense de microprocesadores avanzados Nvidia logró un beneficio neto de 65.287 millones de dólares (unos 59.335 millones de euros) en su tercer trimestre fiscal, comprendido entre finales de julio y finales de octubre, lo que supone elevar sus ganancias en un 105% respecto al año anterior y superar los pronosticos de los analistas, en sus primeras cuentas trimestrales con Jensen Huang fuera de la directiva tras saltar el escándalo relacionado con sus infidelidades. De su lado, los ingresos de la firma alcanzaron los 115.844 millones de dólares (105.282 millones de euros), un incremento del 103% en comparación a hace doce meses. Las acciones de Nvidia cerraron prácticamente planas en los 155,46 dólares (-0,48%) este martes previo a la presentación de resultados, en una jornada marcada además por el anuncio de declaración de Huang ante el Congreso de Estados Unidos y ante la declaración de intenciones del recién dimitido CEO sobre su voluntad de volver al cargo. La junta directiva de Nvidia no contempla restituir a Huang como CEO de la compañía THE OBJECTIVE Sin embargo, los títulos de la compañía ha llegado a repuntar hasta un 3,5% en el mercado after hours una vez desveladas las cuentas trimestrales que ha superado las previsiones de los mercados.

recent_candidates.title: Ocho inmigrantes subsaharianos acceden a Ceuta tras saltar la valla con Marruecos
recent_candidates.author: THE OBJECTIVE
recent_candidates.excerpt: Ocho inmigrantes subsaharianos han accedido irregularmente a Ceuta en las últimas horas tras superar la doble valla que separa la ciudad de Marruecos . Según fuentes policiales consultadas por EFE, realizaron el salto por diferentes puntos de los 8,2 kilómetros del perímetro fronterizo. Todos ellos, en su mayoría jóvenes, se encuentran en buen estado de salud. Los inmigrantes proceden de varios países como Guinea, Sudán y Mali y todos ellos se dirigieron hacia el Centro de Estancia Temporal de Inmigrantes (CETI) tras realizar el salto de la valla fronteriza sin ser detenidos por los agentes de la Guardia Civil que custodian el perímetro. Las entradas se han producido en unos momentos donde se había reducido la presión inmigratoria por el vallado , a pesar de que se siguen registrando accesos puntuales tanto por la vía marítima como por la terrestre.
